ideas.title: Grain-boundary-diffusion Dy-lean magnets cut heavy rare-earth 44% line
ideas.technicalDescription: The 12× NdFeB N42 magnet segments at €214.68 are 44% of the whole motor (E9, E35). The dominant cost driver inside them is heavy rare-earth (Dy/Tb) added in bulk to hold coercivity at the 180°C rotor operating point. Replace bulk-alloyed N42SH-equivalent grade with a grain-boundary-diffusion (GBD) processed magnet: Dy/Tb is diffused only along grain boundaries from a surface source, delivering equivalent HcJ at roughly one-third the heavy-RE content. At Dy₂O₃ 275 €/kg and Tb₄O₇ 1,040 €/kg, cutting heavy-RE loading ~60-70% removes a disproportionate share of the €214.68. GBD is proven at production scale (Shin-Etsu, TDK, Proterial). This pairs naturally with the segmented-magnet cooling precedent — better cooling lowers the coercivity demand, letting GBD go leaner still. Requires re-validation of demag margin at 16,000 rpm / short-circuit fault and thermal soak, plus BH-curve re-characterisation for the FEA torque-ripple model (E33). Magnet geometry, V-slot and rotor lamination are unchanged, so tooling is carried over. Qualify dual-source to hedge rare-earth volatility (E35).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: No change to rotor stamping, V-slot geometry or magnet insertion — GBD is a magnet-supplier process, so the EDU line is untouched. Incoming inspection adds a coercivity/demag audit per lot. Requires re-running rotor demagnetisation FEA and a short-circuit + high-temp soak validation campaign. Dual-sourcing GBD-capable suppliers (Shin-Etsu, TDK, Proterial, VAC) protects against single-source and rare-earth spikes. Magnet drawing revised for HcJ spec and diffusion process note; PPAP re-run on the rotor sub-assembly.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — attacks the single largest cost line via its most expensive constituent
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €214.68 magnet line × ~20% avg net magnet cost reduction from ~60% heavy-RE cut × 200,000 units

ideas.riskNotes: Primary risk is irreversible demagnetisation under short-circuit fault or thermal soak if GBD coercivity margin is mis-specified — an ASIL-B torque-security concern (E32). Mitigate with worst-case fault FEA, over-temperature demag testing, and a coercivity floor in the incoming spec. Leaner heavy-RE can shift BH temperature coefficient, risking order-24 torque ripple drift (E33); re-characterise BH curve and re-tune skew. EU Battery/ELV recycled-content pressure favours lower-RE designs. Dual-source qualification de-risks rare-earth price volatility.

ideas.title: Cut magnet segment count from 12 by improving rotor cooling
ideas.technicalDescription: The rotor uses 12× magnet segments (E9) — segmentation exists purely to break the eddy-current path and limit magnet self-heating at 16,000 rpm with 2 kHz PWM harmonics (E29, E33). Each additional segmentation cut adds wire-EDM/slice cost, handling and adhesive-bonding interfaces per pole. If the oil-spray rotor cooling (E30) is upgraded to a rotor-shaft oil-fed sleeve/channel (transferring the validated rotor-sleeve cooling precedent), magnet operating temperature drops, allowing coarser segmentation — e.g. 12→8 or 12→6 segments per pole set — because the eddy-loss thermal ceiling is relaxed. Fewer cuts = fewer slicing operations, fewer bond lines, faster magnetise-and-insert. This is an architecture move at the rotor sub-assembly: it removes interfaces that exist only because two (many) magnet pieces exist. Combined with GBD magnets it compounds — cooler rotor + boundary-diffused coercivity lets both levers relax. Validation: re-run coupled electromagnetic-thermal FEA for eddy loss vs segment count, verify demag margin, and confirm bond-line shear at 16,000 rpm centrifugal load and 300,000 km fatigue (E32, E34).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Fewer wire-EDM/dicing passes per magnet blank cuts magnet-supplier machining time and adhesive metering per pole. Rotor magnetise-and-insert station handles fewer, larger segments — shorter cycle time and fewer pick-place moves. Requires the rotor oil-sleeve cooling feature (added machining/channel in shaft or rotor pack). Adhesive cure and dispensing recipe re-qualified for larger bond area. New coupled thermal-EM FEA sign-off and centrifugal spin test at 16,000 rpm plus over-speed.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — reduces per-segment machining and handling on the 44% magnet line
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €214.68 magnet line × ~9% avg from ~40% fewer segmentation cuts + faster insert × 200,000, net of rotor cooling feature cost

ideas.riskNotes: Coarser segmentation raises eddy-current loss and local magnet temperature — if cooling under-delivers, demag risk breaches ASIL-B torque security (E32) and NVH/loss targets slip. Mitigate with coupled EM-thermal FEA, oil-flow CFD and instrumented rotor thermocouple validation. Larger bond lines must survive 16,000 rpm centrifugal + thermal-cycle fatigue over 300,000 km (E32, E34); qualify adhesive shear and add retention feature if margin is thin. Cooling-feature machining adds cost that must net positive.

ideas.title: Consolidate 3-part housing into single HPDC water-jacket casting
ideas.technicalDescription: Housing is €47.67 / 9.8% across 3 part instances / 9.8 kg (E5, E11), with the water-jacket housing the €27.39 line (E11). A 3-piece housing implies a jacket shell, an end/cover interface and joining hardware — each bolted or sealed interface exists only because the parts are separate. Consolidate to a single high-pressure die-cast A380 (2,850 €/t) housing with a cast-in spiral water jacket produced by lost-core or cast-in tube, eliminating one machined interface, its O-ring/gasket groove and its fastener set. Target 3 instances → 1 casting plus one machined bearing-carrier cover. This deletes sealing surfaces (a warranty leak-path), joining labour at German rates (£38-47/hr), and stock-keeping of two part numbers. Machine only the bearing bores, stator-fit bore and coolant ports in one fixturing. Cast-in-jacket is standard practice (Bosch, ZF, Valeo eAxle housings). Validate: coolant pressure/burst test, thermal-cycle leak, stone-chip and salt-spray on the exterior (E32) — HPDC A380 needs cataphoretic/powder coat or Mg-free alloy plus sealing for corrosion.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Replaces multi-piece housing assembly (align, seal, bolt, leak-test each joint) with one HPDC casting cell plus a single CNC fixturing for bores and ports. Removes one gasket/O-ring, ~6-10 fasteners and one leak-test interface. HPDC tool is a significant new investment (multi-slide die + lost core or cast-in tube). Coolant passage moves from assembled channel to cast passage — one burst/leak test instead of several. Reduces part numbers and inbound logistics from 3 to ~2. Coating line unchanged if cataphoretic already present.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — attacks the 9.8% housing block via interface deletion and joining labour
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €47.67 housing block × ~20% (deleted joining labour, sealing, one part number) × 200,000, net of amortised HPDC tool

ideas.riskNotes: Cast-in water jacket risks porosity-driven coolant leak into the stator cavity — a durability failure over 15yr/300,000 km (E32). Mitigate with vacuum-assisted HPDC, X-ray/CT porosity gating and 100% burst-leak test. Exterior must survive salt-spray + stone-chip (E32): specify low-Cu A380 or apply cataphoretic + topcoat, avoid Cr6 per REACH. Single casting concentrates NVH transfer path — verify order-24 and 2 kHz radiated noise unchanged (E33) via modal/FRF test. Large die = high NRE; justify on 200,000×5-7yr volume.

ideas.title: Weld phase busbars directly into hairpin crown, delete connection block
ideas.technicalDescription: Power connection is €11.22 / 2.3% across 3 instances / 0.66 kg (E7, E13) — three phase busbars (E13) that exist as a separate sub-assembly only to bridge from the hairpin winding terminals (E4, E10) to the inverter interface. In a hairpin stator the phase-lead crown already presents copper terminals; a discrete busbar block adds a copper part, an insulation carrier, and two joint interfaces (busbar-to-hairpin and busbar-to-terminal). Integrate by forming the phase interconnect directly from the hairpin crown geometry and laser-welding a short integrated bus tab, deleting the standalone busbar carrier and one joint per phase. Copper is 11,700 €/t and Hairpin Cu profile 14.5 €/kg, so mass and joint count both fall. This is an interface-elimination move: the busbar exists because the winding and inverter are two parts — fold the interconnect into the winding crown so only the inverter terminal joint remains. Validate: laser-weld peel/pull strength, high-voltage isolation (800V, partial-discharge), thermal cycling of the joint, and vibration endurance to 300,000 km (E32). NVH unaffected (E33).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Removes the busbar carrier moulding, its assembly/clip station and one laser-weld/ultrasonic joint per phase. Hairpin crown forming tool revised to add integrated bus tabs. One weld interface per phase deleted (3 joints saved). Fewer part numbers into the stator line and less inbound logistics. Requires updated welding fixture and HV isolation test recipe. Insulation strategy shifts to conformal coating/paper on the crown rather than a moulded carrier.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — small block but high fraction removable via interface deletion
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €11.22 block × ~30% (deleted carrier + 3 joints + copper mass) × 200,000

ideas.riskNotes: Integrated bus tabs must hold 800V isolation and partial-discharge limits with tighter creepage/clearance than a moulded carrier provided — mitigate with conformal HV coating and PD test per lot. Weld-joint fatigue at the winding crown under thermal + vibration must survive 300,000 km (E32); qualify pull-strength and cyclic testing. ASIL-B torque path depends on phase continuity (E32) — 100% resistance/continuity test each joint. Loss of a discrete busbar reduces field-repair flexibility; acceptable at module-replace service model.

ideas.title: Swap resolver for PCB inductive position sensor
ideas.technicalDescription: Sensing is €9.5 / 2% (E8, E14), the resolver being the single line at bought-part €9.50 (E14). A wound resolver is a legacy component: copper windings, a laminated stator/rotor, precision air-gap alignment, and a dedicated RDC (resolver-to-digital converter) in the inverter. Replace with a printed-circuit inductive position sensor (e.g. Renesas/Microchip IPS, ZF/Melexis inductive rotor-position sensors) — a stamped/etched copper coil on a thin PCB target, no laminations, no windings, tolerant of air-gap and eccentricity, and directly digital so the RDC circuit deletes from the inverter (E27, unpriced). Bought-part cost of an inductive sensor is typically 30-50% below a resolver, and it removes a precision-alignment station. It is ASIL-B/D capable with dual-channel redundancy for torque security (E32). This is an architecture move at the sensing sub-assembly: it collapses the resolver + RDC into one PCB sensor and frees inverter PCB area (the deleted RDC is on the not-costed inverter row, so that portion is unpriced per E27). Validate accuracy vs order-24 ripple mapping (E33), EMC at 2 kHz PWM, and temperature drift to 180°C.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Deletes the resolver's precision air-gap alignment/calibration station and its wound component supply. Inductive sensor mounts as a flat PCB with relaxed positional tolerance, cutting assembly time and scrap from mis-alignment. Removes the RDC circuit from the inverter PCB (unpriced, E27), freeing board area and one supply part. Requires new sensor calibration routine, EMC re-validation against 2 kHz PWM, and firmware update to the motor controller for angle decoding. One bought-part number swapped, simpler inbound logistics.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — removes most of a 2% block plus unpriced inverter RDC deletion
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €9.5 sensing block × ~35% bought-part delta + alignment labour saved × 200,000; inverter RDC deletion unpriced per E27

ideas.riskNotes: Position-sensing accuracy is safety-critical (ASIL-B torque security, E32) — inductive sensors must be qualified dual-channel with plausibility checks; validate accuracy across 0-16,000 rpm and 180°C. Angle error can excite order-24 torque ripple and 2 kHz whine (E33); characterise error harmonics and compensate in firmware. EMC susceptibility to PWM fields must be proven (shielded PCB, differential coils). Temperature drift and long-term stability over 300,000 km require accelerated-life testing. Supplier maturity is high (Renesas, Melexis, ZF).

ideas.title: Commonise one stator diameter, vary stack length across variants
ideas.technicalDescription: Stator lamination stack is €30.63 / 6.3% / 12 kg (E6, E12) using Si Steel M270 (2,400 €/t, lam 3.4 €/kg). The dominant cost lever at 200,000/yr over 5-7 years (E36) is tooling amortisation and the per-variant NRE of separate lamination dies. Adopt a scalable-length family architecture: fix the stator/rotor outer diameter and slot geometry, and vary only stack length to cover the D-segment power spread (e.g. 200-300 kW variants) — exactly the Audi PPE / Mercedes eATS 2.0 / XPeng SEPA2.0 route where ~80% of parts are shared. One progressive lamination die, one winding-crown tool, one rotor stamping die serve all variants; stack count changes on the same tooling. This commonisation move spreads a single tool set across far higher cumulative volume, lowering amortised piece price on the lamination stack, hairpin winding tool and rotor die simultaneously. It also cuts spare-part and PPAP proliferation. Validate: electromagnetic scaling holds torque/ripple targets at each length (E33), and thermal derating maps re-computed per stack (E30). No new material or process — purely architecture and tooling strategy.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Single lamination progressive die, single hairpin former and single rotor die run all power variants by changing stack height only — massive tooling NRE avoidance versus per-variant dies. Line changeover between variants is a stack-count parameter, not a re-tool. Reduces active part numbers, PPAP submissions and spares inventory. Requires up-front architecture lock and a common outer-diameter decision across the programme's variant plan. Winding insertion parameterised by stack length. One coating/impregnation recipe scales across lengths.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — amortises stator/rotor/winding tooling across the whole variant family
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Avoided per-variant die NRE (2-3 variants × ~€3-5M dies) amortised over 200,000×5-7yr + lower per-piece tool cost on €30.63 + €81.53 lines

ideas.riskNotes: Fixing one diameter forces a compromise efficiency/NVH optimum across variants — a longer stack may shift order-24 ripple or 2 kHz whine at certain operating points (E33); mitigate with per-length skew and control-map tuning. Over-constraining diameter can leave the top variant thermally limited (E30); verify continuous-power derating at max stack. Programme risk if variant plan changes mid-cycle. Requires cross-programme governance to hold the common architecture; strong precedent (Audi PPE, Mercedes eATS 2.0) de-risks feasibility.

ideas.title: Cast rotor end-plates with integral balancing bosses
ideas.technicalDescription: The rotor block is €301.53 / 61.9% across 16 part instances (E3, E9, E15). Beyond magnets, the instance count implies discrete rotor end-plates, balance rings/weights, retaining rings and shaft interface parts — each adding a machined component and a stack-and-fix interface. Consolidate the non-magnet rotor hardware: replace separate steel end-plates + bolted balance rings with die-cast/forged aluminium end-plates that integrate the magnet-retention shoulder and pre-formed balancing bosses (material removed at balance, not weights added). This cuts part instances, deletes retaining-ring and balance-weight interfaces, and reduces rotor mass — directly benefiting inertia for launch response (E34). Lower rotating mass also eases the centrifugal load on magnet bond lines. Aluminium (2,700 €/t) end-plates replace heavier steel plus bolt-on weights. This is an architecture move within the 16-instance rotor: interfaces that exist only because retention and balancing are separate parts are folded into one cast plate. Validate: burst/over-speed at 16,000 rpm (E29), balance grade G2.5 achievable by material removal, magnet-retention under centrifugal + thermal cycling (E32), and rotor-dynamic critical speed unchanged for NVH (E33).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Replaces multiple machined end-plates, retaining rings and bolt-on balance weights with two cast/forged aluminium end-plates carrying integral retention shoulders and balance bosses. Balancing shifts from adding weights to milling material off the bosses — a faster, cleaner balance operation. Fewer rotor-stack part numbers and fewer fastening/staking steps. Requires new end-plate casting/forging tool and a spin-balance cell recipe change. Over-speed burst validation per lot sampling. Rotor stack press/retain sequence simplified.

ideas.title: Optimise V-magnet geometry to cut magnet mass 8-12%
ideas.technicalDescription: Magnets are 44% of the motor and the board-level supply risk (E9, E35). Beyond material grade, magnet *volume* is set by the V-shaped buried-magnet flux design (E31). Re-optimise the rotor magnetic circuit with modern topology tools: asymmetric/stepped V-slot geometry, flux-barrier tuning and a partial iron-bridge redesign to raise magnet utilisation, targeting equal 480 Nm / 250 kW (E29) at 8-12% less NdFeB mass. Techniques proven in production include tapered magnet pockets, delta/double-V layering and optimised bridge saturation to concentrate flux where it produces torque. Because magnets are the dominant line, an 8-12% volume cut yields large absolute saving even at N42 92 €/kg. This is a design/architecture lever on the rotor lamination and magnet blank sizing — it also lowers rotor inertia (E34) and reduces the demag-vulnerable magnet mass. It stacks with GBD-magnet and cooling ideas. Validate: torque-ripple order-24 must not rise from the revised barrier geometry (E33), demag margin at fault (E32), and manufacturability of thinner iron bridges under centrifugal load at 16,000 rpm (E29).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Rotor lamination progressive die revised for the new V-slot/barrier geometry; magnet blank size reduced (thinner or shorter segments) cutting sintered NdFeB volume purchased. No new process — same stamp, insert, bond, magnetise flow with re-sized parts. Requires extensive electromagnetic + structural FEA and prototype dyno correlation. Iron-bridge thinning must be checked for stamping burr and fatigue. Magnet supplier drawing and rotor die both change; one PPAP cycle on the rotor sub-assembly.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — direct volume cut on the single largest cost line
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €214.68 magnet line × ~10% mass reduction × 200,000 (NdFeB N42 at 92 €/kg)

ideas.riskNotes: Reducing magnet volume erodes demag margin and can drop peak torque at high temperature — ASIL-B torque security (E32) requires validated worst-case fault + thermal demag testing. Revised flux barriers directly shape order-24 torque ripple and 2 kHz whine (E33), a top-three complaint driver — extensive NVH FEA and dyno correlation mandatory, with skew retuning. Thinner iron bridges raise centrifugal-stress risk at 16,000 rpm (E29); verify fatigue and stamping quality. Best combined with GBD magnets to preserve coercivity headroom.

ideas.title: Grain-boundary diffusion cuts heavy rare-earth in magnets
ideas.technicalDescription: The magnet line is €214.68 (44% of the motor, E9/E16). Baseline V-buried magnets are almost certainly N42-class sintered NdFeB carrying blended (bulk) Dy/Tb for coercivity at the 16,000 rpm/high-temp duty. Switch the supplier route to grain-boundary diffusion (GBD) processing, where Dy/Tb is diffused only along grain boundaries of a low-heavy-RE base (e.g. N45UH via GBD) rather than alloyed through the bulk. GBD delivers equivalent Hcj (intrinsic coercivity) at 30-60% less Dy/Tb by mass. With Dy2O3 at €275/kg and Tb4O7 at €1,040/kg versus NdPr oxide at €79/kg, the heavy-RE fraction dominates magnet cost. A typical 150°C-rated traction magnet carries 1.5-3% Dy; halving that via GBD on the same N-grade base saves meaningful €/kg on 1.8 kg of magnet. The V-shape geometry and 12-segment count are unchanged, so rotor lamination pockets, adhesive and balancing are untouched. Requires re-qualification of BH curve at 180°C, demag pulse test, and IEC 60404 flux measurement per lot. Combine with the verified rotor-sleeve cooling lever to further lower the required operating Hcj, compounding the Dy reduction.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: No change to rotor stack assembly, magnet insertion or adhesive process — the segment envelope and 12x count are preserved, so no rotor tooling change. Change is entirely at the magnet supplier: GBD is an added post-sinter diffusion + ageing step, already in volume production at Hitachi, Shin-Etsu and JL MAG. PPAP requires new magnetic characterisation (open-circuit flux, recoil permeability, knee-point at max operating temp) and a demagnetisation-withstand test after the worst-case short-circuit current pulse. Dual-source the GBD grade to manage rare-earth supply risk (E35).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — attacks the single largest cost line via the most expensive element
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €214.68 magnet line × 12-20% reduction from ~50% Dy/Tb cut × 200,000 units

ideas.riskNotes: Primary risk is thermal demagnetisation at the 180°C rotor hotspot and after an ASIL-B short-circuit event (E32). GBD magnets have a shallower Dy gradient, so surface Hcj is highest — advantageous for surface eddy losses but requires demag-pulse validation. NVH (order-24 ripple, E33) is unaffected as remanence and geometry are held. Mitigate with worst-case magnetic FEA plus physical demag pulse testing and lot-level flux screening. Supply concentration in China remains; dual-source and honour EU battery/critical-raw-material traceability.
dfmaPrinciples: Design to function not to margin

ideas.regulatoryContext: Supports EU Critical Raw Materials Act intent by cutting heavy-rare-earth dependency and improves battery/motor passport material declarations.

ideas.title: Reduce magnet mass via optimised V-angle and flux-focusing
ideas.technicalDescription: Magnets are 44% of motor cost and 1.8 kg (E9/E16). The single most direct lever on the €214.68 line is removing magnet mass while holding torque (480 Nm) and airgap flux density. Re-optimise the 8-pole V-buried geometry: increase the V-opening angle and add flux-barrier bridges to concentrate flux, and thin each segment (reduce radial thickness) rather than deleting segments. Modern topology optimisation (JMAG/Motor-CAD with genetic algorithms) routinely recovers 8-15% magnet mass at equal torque by improving PM utilisation factor and reducing flux leakage through the iron bridges. A 12% mass cut on 1.8 kg NdFeB at N42 blended cost is directly proportional to the €214.68 line. Because the rotor lamination pockets change, this requires a new rotor lamination die (progressive/Si-steel M270) — a real tooling consequence of ~€250-400k — but amortised over 200,000/yr × 7 yr it is trivial. Torque ripple must be co-optimised: asymmetric V-angle and pole-shaping (step-skew already assumed) let magnet reduction proceed without raising order-24 ripple. Also lowers rotor inertia, aiding launch response (E34).

ideas.title: Ferrite-assisted synchronous rotor cuts NdFeB dependency
ideas.technicalDescription: Rare-earth price volatility is a board-level supply risk (E35) and magnets are 44% of motor cost (E9). A structural hedge is a PM-assisted synchronous reluctance (PMa-SynRM) or hybrid rotor that replaces a portion of NdFeB with low-cost ferrite (Sr-ferrite ~€3-5/kg vs N42 €92/kg) placed in the reluctance flux barriers. The reluctance torque component carries base load; ferrite provides field to lift power factor and reduce controller current, with a small NdFeB fraction retained for the high-speed field-weakening region. This can remove 40-60% of NdFeB mass. Because ferrite has ~1/3 the remanence, the rotor diameter/stack must grow slightly or a multi-barrier lamination adopted, meaning a full new rotor lamination design and die (Si-steel M270, €300-450k). Torque ripple in SynRM/PMa topologies is inherently higher, so a multi-layer barrier design with rotor step-skew is mandatory to protect order-24 NVH (E33). This is a strategic decoupling from the Dy/Nd market more than a pure piece-price play, but at €92/kg NdFeB the material arbitrage is real even after the larger stack.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a completely new rotor lamination geometry (multi-barrier), new progressive die, revised magnet inventory (ferrite blocks + reduced NdFeB), and new balancing/skew fixtures. Ferrite is brittle and inserted as pressed blocks — insertion and retention tooling differs from sintered NdFeB. Stator and windings may need rewind for the altered saliency ratio. Extensive EM, thermal and NVH re-validation and ASIL-B torque-security re-proof. Higher engineering NRE but structurally lower and more stable material cost across the 7-year programme.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — large material arbitrage offset by bigger stack and NVH engineering
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 40-60% NdFeB substitution to ferrite on €214.68 line, net of larger lamination/copper, × 200,000

ideas.riskNotes: PMa-SynRM has intrinsically higher torque ripple and acoustic risk directly against NVH complaint driver (E33); ferrite risks demagnetisation at low temperature (opposite of NdFeB). Larger stack raises inertia, opposing launch-response goal (E34). Power factor and field-weakening at 16,000 rpm (E29) must be re-verified. Mitigate with multi-barrier skewed rotor, low-temp demag validation, and controller re-tune. ASIL-B (E32) requires full re-characterisation. Highest-risk, highest-strategic-value option.

ideas.title: Flow-formed hollow rotor shaft cuts cost and inertia
ideas.technicalDescription: The rotor shaft is €61.67 and 3.2 kg (E18), the second-largest single rotor line after magnets. If baseline is a machined-from-solid or forged 42CrMo4 shaft, switch to a flow-formed / rotary-swaged hollow shaft from a seamless tube blank. Flow-forming produces near-net-shape thin-wall hollow shafts with excellent concentricity and work-hardened surface, removing large volumes of turning stock and cutting cycle time and material buy-to-fly ratio dramatically. For an 800V oil-spray-cooled rotor (E30), a hollow shaft is doubly valuable because it becomes the oil-feed gallery for rotor/magnet cooling, directly synergistic with the verified rotor-sleeve cooling lever. Mass drops ~25-35% (0.8-1.1 kg off 3.2 kg), reducing rotor inertia for launch response (E34). Machining reduces to finish-turning of bearing journals and splining. Requires a flow-forming line or supplier (Leico/WF Maschinenbau process), new mandrels, and rotor-to-shaft interference-fit/weld re-validation at 16,000 rpm (E29). Torsional stiffness for ASIL-B torque transmission (E32) must be re-proven, but hollow shafts are standard in premium EDUs.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Move from bar-stock turning to tube-blank flow-forming + finish machining. New forming mandrels and tooling (~€150-300k) plus finish-turning fixtures. Balancing benefits from lower mass and improved concentricity. Rotor-stack-to-shaft joining (shrink-fit or laser weld) revalidated for the thinner wall. Oil gallery drilling deleted if the bore serves cooling. Reduced raw-material purchase and chip scrap improves plant material yield and cost per part.

ideas.title: Thinner high-Si laminations plus bonded stack, closed scrap loop
ideas.technicalDescription: Stator lamination stack is €30.63 / 12 kg (E12/E19) and rotor lamination €16.78 / 6.5 kg (E22) — together ~€47 and 18.5 kg of Si steel at €3.4/kg. Two combined levers: (1) move from assumed 0.30-0.35 mm M270 to thinner 0.20-0.25 mm high-silicon grade (e.g. NO20/M235) to cut iron and eddy loss — this raises €/kg but the loss reduction lets the stack shorten slightly at equal output, and at 800V/SiC high-fundamental-frequency operation the efficiency gain is real; (2) capture and sell/re-melt the punching skeleton scrap under a closed-loop contract with the Si-steel mill, recovering value on the ~40-50% scrap fraction inherent to annular lamination blanking. On 200,000 units × 18.5 kg × 40% scrap = ~1,480 t/yr of prompt scrap; a toll/buy-back at even €1.5/kg over open-market recovers material cost. Also evaluate laser-cut or bonded (backlack self-bonding) stacks to eliminate welding/interlock burrs that raise iron loss and NVH. Backlack bonding lowers audible whine (E33) by damping inter-lamination movement.

Backlack self-bonding replaces interlock/weld with an in-die adhesive-cure step. The scrap-loop lever is purely commercial/logistics: install skeleton baling and a mill buy-back agreement. Higher press wear at thin gauge managed with carbide tooling. Iron-loss and NVH re-validation required for the gauge and bonding change.

Bond-line failure would degrade stack stiffness and NVH (E33). Mitigate with adhesive thermal-ageing qualification and shear testing. Thinner laminations improve efficiency but reduce stack mechanical robustness — verify buckling and press-fit retention. Scrap buy-back price is market-linked and must be contractually floored to protect the saving.

ideas.title: Continuous wave-wound hairpins delete weld count and copper
ideas.technicalDescription: Hairpin winding set is €81.53 / 4.5 kg (E10/E17), the largest single windings line and 17.7% of the motor. Conventional I-pin/X-pin construction inserts many discrete U-pins and laser-welds every crown pair — dozens of welds per stator, each a cost, quality and NVH risk. Move to a continuous wave-winding (formed from a small number of long pre-shaped conductors, e.g. Vitesco/Schaeffler continuous-hairpin or 'wave winding') that halves or better the number of laser welds and reduces end-turn copper (shorter, tighter end-turns). Fewer welds cut laser-weld station time and rework; shorter end-turns cut copper mass on 4.5 kg at Hairpin Cu Profile €14.5/kg. Continuous winding also improves slot-fill and thermal path, helping the water-jacket duty (E30). Requires new winding-forming tooling and insertion equipment (significant NRE, €1-2M line change) but at 200,000/yr × 7 yr amortises fast. Weld reduction directly reduces a top NVH/quality risk area and the 2 kHz PWM whine path via more consistent end-turn geometry (E33).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Replaces discrete hairpin insertion + full weld matrix with continuous-conductor forming, insertion and a reduced weld set. Major stator winding line retool: new forming mandrels, insertion heads, and fewer laser-weld positions. Reduces weld inspection burden and scrap. Copper purchase drops with shorter end-turns. Requires full electrical (partial-discharge at 800V), thermal and NVH re-validation and IATF PPAP of the new winding topology.

ideas.title: Replace resolver with commonised inductive position sensor
ideas.technicalDescription: The resolver is €9.50 (E14/E24) — small in share (2%) but a pure bought-part with a proven cheaper substitute and a strong commonisation angle. Replace the classical wound resolver + resolver-to-digital converter with a printed inductive (eddy-current) position sensor (e.g. Renesas/Melexis/ Microchip LX34070-class or Vitesco inductive) that uses a stamped-metal target and a PCB coil, delivering ASIL-B-capable absolute angle at lower piece cost and lower mass/height. The bigger prize is commonisation: specify one inductive sensor + target family across both front and rear EDUs and across the scalable motor-length family (KB lever 2/4), consolidating one part number and one supplier across the whole BEV platform. This is an unpriced-magnitude commonisation saving beyond the €9.50 piece delta, since it removes a variant and its validation. ASIL-B torque-security path (E32) is preserved with a certified inductive device.

Simplifies harness (fewer dedicated sensor wires) and one connector. ideas.title: Grain-boundary-diffused NdFeB cuts heavy rare-earth loading
ideas.technicalDescription: The 12× NdFeB magnet segments at €214.68 (44% of the motor, E9/E16) carry Dy/Tb dispersed through the bulk to hold coercivity at the 180°C rotor-cooled operating point. Switch from bulk-alloyed N42EH to grain-boundary-diffusion (GBD) processed N42UH/EH grade, where Dy₂O₃ (€275/kg) or Tb₄O₇ (€1,040/kg) is applied only to the grain boundaries by sputter/slurry diffusion. GBD delivers equivalent 20+ kOe intrinsic coercivity with 40-60% less heavy rare-earth by mass, because HRE concentrates where reverse-domain nucleation actually initiates. On a 1.8 kg magnet set with ~2-3% Dy/Tb baseline loading, cutting HRE by half removes roughly €12-18 of the segment price without touching remanence (Br) — so torque density, back-EMF and order-24 ripple (E33) are unchanged. Requires re-qualification of demagnetisation curve at 150/180°C, PWM ripple-loss eddy heating and 15-year/300,000 km thermal-ageing (E32). Segment count (12×) and V-shape geometry (E31) are carried over, so rotor lamination tooling is untouched. Combine with oil-spray rotor cooling headroom (E30) to run a lower HRE grade safely.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: No change to segmentation, magnetising fixtures or rotor slot geometry — GBD is a magnet-supplier process step upstream of the OEM. Incoming inspection adds a coercivity-vs-temperature check and a per-lot HRE assay to guard against diffusion-depth drift. Adhesive bonding and corrosion coating (Ni-Cu-Ni / epoxy) of segments unchanged. Dual-sourcing GBD magnets (JL MAG, Shin-Etsu, Yantai Zhenghai) protects against the board-level rare-earth supply risk in E35. PPAP requires new demag and salt-spray data.

ideas.title: Partial Ce substitution in NdFeB lowers NdPr content
ideas.technicalDescription: The magnet set is 44% of motor cost and rare-earth price is a board-level risk (E35). Beyond heavy-rare-earth reduction, substitute a portion of Nd/Pr with cerium (Ce), the cheapest and most abundant light rare earth, using a dual-alloy / dual-main-phase sintering route. NdPr oxide runs €79/kg (live sheet); Ce is a fraction of that and is a by-product surplus of the mining stream. A 10-20% Ce-for-NdPr substitution in a Ce-NdFeB dual-main-phase magnet holds Br within 3-5% and coercivity adequate for a buried-magnet rotor with oil-spray cooling headroom (E30/E31). On the 1.8 kg, €214.68 set (E16), a 15% NdPr substitution could remove €8-14/set. The V-shaped buried geometry (E31) is more tolerant of a small remanence drop than a surface-magnet design because reluctance torque contributes a share of the 480 Nm. Requires re-tuning magnet thickness or slight remanence compensation to hold back-EMF at 16,000 rpm, plus full demag and NVH re-validation to protect order-24 ripple (E33). Keeps 12× segmentation and existing magnetiser.

Because Ce grades are less corrosion-robust, confirm the Ni-Cu-Ni + epoxy coating passes salt-spray (E32). ideas.title: Optimise magnet segmentation from 12 to 8 segments
ideas.technicalDescription: Segmentation of the buried magnets (12× per pole-set, E16) is done to suppress eddy-current losses in the magnet body driven by 2 kHz PWM ripple and slot-harmonic flux (E33). With an 800V SiC inverter the switching frequency can be raised and ripple current reduced, and with oil-spray rotor cooling (E30) the eddy heat is actively removed — both slacken the segmentation requirement. Re-run a coupled electromagnetic-thermal loss model to find the minimum axial+circumferential cut count that holds magnet eddy loss and hotspot temperature within limit; a move from 12 to 8 segments per set is realistic. Fewer, larger segments reduce coating surface area (less Ni-Cu-Ni per kg), dicing operations and assembly insertions, and modestly improve pack density. Magnet mass and grade unchanged, so Br/torque and order-24 ripple (E33) are preserved by design intent — only the eddy-loss margin is spent. Saving is a conversion-cost reduction (~€1.5-3/set) rather than raw material, so it is priced modestly.

ideas.title: Thinner 0.20mm Si-steel lamination cuts iron loss and mass
ideas.technicalDescription: The stator lamination stack (€30.63, 12 kg, E19) and rotor lamination stack (€16.78, 6.5 kg, E22) are priced on Si-steel at €3.4/kg. The stated concern is 2 kHz PWM whine and iron loss (E33). Move from a typical 0.27-0.35 mm non-oriented grade (e.g. M270-35A) to a thinner 0.20 mm high-silicon grade (e.g. 20JNEH1200 / NO20). Thinner laminations cut classical eddy-current iron loss (which scales with the square of sheet thickness), directly reducing the high-frequency loss that the SiC 800V inverter's fast switching excites (E29) and improving continuous-rating efficiency. Thinner sheet also allows a slightly shorter stack for the same flux, trimming mass on the rotor (inertia, E34). This is a grade substitution, not a geometry change: existing progressive-die lamination tooling accepts the thinner strip with feed and clearance re-set. The premium of 0.20 mm grade (~+15-25%/kg) is partially offset by shorter stack length and is justified where efficiency and NVH (E33) carry booked value. Blanking burr and stacking factor must be re-controlled; interlock/bond-varnish stacking re-validated.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Progressive stamping die runs thinner strip — die clearance, feed and de-stacking re-tuned; more laminations per stack means higher press stroke count and slightly longer stacking cycle. Backlack/bonding or self-clinch interlock re-qualified for the thinner sheet. Stacking factor drops slightly, requiring stack-height compensation. Higher-Si grade is more brittle — monitor blanking burr and tool wear. No new press; tooling refresh only.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — efficiency/NVH value, material near-neutral
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Shorter stack mass saving + efficiency-credit; net €2-4.5/motor across two stacks

ideas.riskNotes: Thinner grade premium can erode material saving if stack cannot be shortened — validate flux density headroom first. More laminations raise stacking-process defect exposure. Brittleness risks blanking cracks lifting scrap. Mitigate with die-clearance DOE and stacking-factor control. NVH re-test mandatory to confirm 2 kHz whine actually falls (E33), not just shifts. Efficiency credit only real if booked in the vehicle energy model.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Lucid Air and Tesla Plaid use 0.20mm-class NO steel for high-rpm efficiency; ArcelorMittal iCARe thin-gauge grades.

ideas.title: Replace resolver with printed inductive position sensor
ideas.technicalDescription: The resolver (E24, €9.50, bought part, 2% of motor, E14) is a wound electromagnetic angle sensor supporting the ASIL-B torque-security requirement (E32) and feeding field-oriented control that governs order-24 torque ripple and PWM whine behaviour (E33). Replace it with a printed-PCB inductive position sensor (eddy-current coupling to a stamped conductive rotor target), which reaches ASIL-C/D functional-safety ratings, tolerates rotor oil-spray and high temperature (E30), and costs materially less because it is a flat multilayer PCB plus a stamped target versus a wound transformer. Inductive sensors also remove the resolver's sensitivity to axial/radial placement tolerance, improving angle accuracy which directly benefits torque-ripple control and NVH (E33). Because this is a bought-part swap, the saving is a purchase-price delta (roughly €3-5 vs €9.50) and is priced as such — the line is user-entered, not engine-costed, so the material/process saving is quantified from supplier catalogue not the engine. Integration requires new ASIL-B safety case sign-off, EMC re-qualification against the SiC PWM environment (E29), and controller software re-calibration of the angle observer.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Sensor becomes a thin PCB mounted at the NDE with a stamped steel target on the shaft end — simpler assembly, no fine-wire resolver winding, laser-trim not required. Supplier base broadens (Melexis, Renesas, Microsemi/Microchip inductive) improving commercial leverage over resolver duopoly. EMC shielding validated against 800V SiC switching. Software calibration and end-of-line angle-learn routine updated. No motor tooling impact.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low absolute but high margin on a small line
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €3-5 purchase-price delta × 200,000 (bought-part, supplier-catalogue basis)

ideas.riskNotes: Position sensing is ASIL-B safety-critical (E32); an angle fault corrupts torque control. Inductive sensors are EMC-sensitive near 800V SiC switching (E29) — validate immunity thoroughly. Any angle-accuracy regression would worsen torque ripple and NVH (E33). Mitigate with full functional-safety case, EMC bench + vehicle test, and back-to-back dyno NVH comparison versus resolver before release.

ideas.title: Common stack diameter, varied length across EDU family
ideas.technicalDescription: The stator lamination (E19), rotor lamination (E22), hairpin winding set (E17) and housing bore (E20) tooling are all diameter-driven. Adopt a scalable-length architecture: fix the lamination outer/inner diameter and the housing bore across the whole EDU family (front/rear axle variants, and any higher/lower-power derivative), and vary only the axial stack length to change torque/power. This lets the €301.53 rotor tooling, the €30.63 stator lamination die (E19) and the housing HPDC die (E20) amortise across every variant at the 200,000/yr × 7-year volume (E36) instead of per-variant tooling. The hairpin winding set (E17, €81.53) reuses the same slot geometry and hairpin bending fixtures, changing only conductor count/length per stack. Because the 8-pole V-magnet topology (E31) and 800V/SiC electrical design (E29) are held constant, the electromagnetic and NVH signature (E33) is characterised once and scaled, cutting validation cost per variant. Saving is tooling amortisation and NRE avoidance across the programme, not a per-part material reduction — so it is priced as amortised tooling/commonisation benefit, unpriced against the single-motor BOM.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: One progressive lamination die, one hairpin bending/insertion set and one housing die serve all variants; only stack-height stops and conductor-cut length change between derivatives. Line changeover between variants becomes a parameter change, not a re-tool, lifting OEE. Winding VPI (E26) and balancing recipes parameterised by length. Enables single-line multi-variant flow. Requires up-front design discipline to freeze the shared diameter.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — amortises the most expensive tooling across the family
costSavingPotential.annualValue: €1.0M–€2.0M/yr amortised NRE avoidance (unpriced vs single BOM)
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Avoided duplicate lamination/housing/winding tooling NRE spread across variants

ideas.riskNotes: Freezing a shared diameter can leave a derivative slightly non-optimal (small efficiency/NVH penalty at one end of the range, E33). Mitigate by choosing the diameter at the volume-weighted optimum and validating the NVH signature at each stack length. Long axial variants risk rotor-dynamics criticals near 16,000 rpm — check each length. Governance risk: variant teams must not re-open the frozen interface.
dfmaPrinciples: Vary one parameter (stack length) for range
ideas.timeToImplement: Architecture decision now; 18-30 months to family rollout
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Mercedes eATS 2.0, Audi PPE and XPeng SEPA2.0 use one diameter with varied stack length; ~80% part sharing.
